sources.used_for: Rounded “Say” dimensions: span 7.4 ft, wrist span 3.7 ft, shoulder span 4 in, maximum body width 8 in, overall length 55 in; paragraph total wing area 6.61 ft²; swan outline and near-parallel inner chord. The stated AR 8.29 is a rounding cross-check.
Qualitative separation of arm/inner and hand/outer wing panels, plus the proposal to use a conventional tail, fin and rudder for an ornithopter.
Selection of rounded fields, conversion policy, exclusions, and interpretation boundaries.

assumptions: Exact conversions use 1 ft = 0.3048 m and 1 in = 0.0254 m. Thus the selected values are span 2.25552 m, wrist span 1.12776 m, shoulder span 0.1016 m, body width 0.2032 m, length 1.397 m, and area 0.6140890944 m².
Aspect ratio is derived as span²/area = 8.284417032 (rounded), consistent with the page's 8.29.
Each individual exposed wing length is inferred as (span − shoulder span)/2 rather than copied from the excluded wing-length row.

For visualization only, the inner panel has an assumed ±18 degree sinusoidal stroke and the outer panel adds an assumed ±26 degree wrist stroke. These make panel articulation legible and are not measured performance data.

The 6 kg mass, aerodynamic polar, 400 W drive, 65% conversion, two-hertz phase, controls, atmosphere, ground contact and landing limits are new benchmark assumptions supplied by the task, not claims made by Stanley J. O. Tinn.
excluded_fields: Page 14 biological stroke-angle reference frames, elastic stiffness discussion, vortex-lift landing hypothesis, and unspecified curved-plate polar.
Any missing appendices, the distinct “Standard Model Swan”, and prior human-carrying simulator designs.
limitations: The photographs are historical notes and observations, not a complete or validated blueprint.
This is a point-mass, cycle-averaged educational model. It is not a structural, unsteady-flow, wake, aeroelastic, stability or biological-flight solver.
Animated panels are visual geometry independent of the cycle-averaged force calculation; powered thrust is an explicit assumption rather than experimentally demonstrated wing performance.
Tail and fin proportions, section thicknesses, hinge geometry, materials and visual colors are illustrative because the sources do not fully specify them.
Publishing a claim of real-world physical validity would require evidence beyond this model and evaluation.
